title: What should replace UDAs? Former CDO lays out an alternative
html:
The LDC Confederation has responded to former chief dental officer (CDO) for England Sara Hurley’s call to replace units of dental activity (UDAs) with a ‘population oral health contract’ which prioritises prevention over cure.

Hurley said that the current UDA-based NHS dental contract ‘rewards treatment after disease has occurred, not prevention before disease escalates’ and needed to be entirely scrapped.

Her recommendation for a replacement is a ‘population oral health contract’ whereby practices would take responsibility for a list of registered patients as their ‘dental home’.

‘NHS dentistry should stop buying activity after disease has occurred and instead commission registered responsibility for the oral health trajectory of a defined population.’ Sara Hurley Former CDO for England

How would the new system replace UDAs?

Under the proposed system, practices would be responsible for helping prevent problems, not just treating you when something goes wrong. As such, preventive care, including fluoride varnish, sealants and help reducing sugar or smoking, would be specifically funded.

Practices serving poorer areas or communities with more dental disease would receive more funding. Urgent appointments would still be available, but should help patients join an ongoing practice afterwards. More complicated treatment would be referred to specialist services, with the regular practice remaining involved.

For practices, Hurley is clear that this additional responsibility should be paired with explicit risk pricing, stable monthly income, protected legitimate costs, paid prevention, funded urgent access, proportionate reconciliation and transition protection.

She stressed that changes should be thoroughly tested on a local level before being rolled out nationally, ensuring that it is affordable, workable for practices, fair for patients, and genuinely improves access.

‘The crisis in NHS dentistry is not simply an access problem. It is a purchasing problem: the NHS is buying activity when it needs to buy responsibility, prevention and continuity.’ Sara Hurley

How would the contract be funded?

Population oral health contract funding would use an annual contract value formula combining:

  • Risk-adjusted registered-population funding
  • Separately paid preventive interventions
  • Protected laboratory costs for routine restorative work
  • Urgent-care capacity and attendance payments
  • A quality premium
  • Deduction of patient-charge income.

Patients would enter four pathways:

  1. Low-risk maintenance
  2. active prevention for elevated risk
  3. Routine restorative/stabilisation care
  4. Complex or specialist care, separately commissioned but coordinated by the dental home.

Does the profession support the proposal to replace UDAs?

Hurley laid out this blueprint in From Probability to Prevention, a document submitted for independent review and policy consultation in July 2026. In November 2026, she reported back from a discussion of the proposal with the local dental committee (LDC) Confederation Board.

The main concerns raised by the LDC include bureaucracy, payment reliability and whether headline national figures discussed in the proposal will work for an individual practice.

Hurley welcomed the challenges presented, saying: ‘From Probability to Prevention is a starting point. The task now is to develop it together, and to put our collective experience to work in shaping reform.’

The proposal was shared with the Department of Health and Social Care and the current CDO ahead of the promised contract consultation, which Hurley notes ‘we are still waiting for’.

When asked if the pledged large-scale reform of the NHS dental contract would be delivered within this Parliamentary term, dental minister James Frith failed to provide a simple yes.

Instead, he said contract reform was a key part of improving access to NHS dentistry without committing to a timeline.
